![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:1/block:1) ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:1/block:2) **OPEN** www.nature.com/scientificreports ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:1/block:5) ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:1/block:6) ![Formula block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:1/block:7) # Critical importance of pH and collector type on the otationof sphalerite and galenafrom a low‑grade lead–zinc ore **Abdolrahim Foroutan**1 **, Majid Abbas Zadeh HajiAbadi**1**,Yaser Kianinia**1 **& Mahdi Ghadiri**2,3\* **Collector type and pulp pH play an important role in the lead–zinc ore otation process. In the current study, the eect of pulp pH and the collector type parameters on the galena and sphalerite otation from a complex lead–zinc–iron ore was investigated.The ethyl xanthate andAero 3418 collectors were used for lead otation andAero 3477 and amyl xanthate for zinc otation. It was found that maximum lead grade could be achieved by usingAero 3418 as collector at pH 8.Also, iron and zinc recoveries and grades were increased in the lead concentrate at lower pH which caused zinc recovery reduction in the zinc concentrate and decrease the lead grade concentrate. Furthermore, the results showed that the maximum zinc grade and recovery of 42.9% and 76.7% were achieved at pH 6 in the presence ofAero 3477 as collector. For both collectors at pH 5, Zinc recovery was increased around 2–3%; however, the iron recovery was also increased at this pH which reduced the zinc concentrate quality. Finally, pH 8 and pH 6 were selected as optimum pH values for lead and zinc otation circuits, respectively.** e Gushl Lead–Zinc mine is located in the Irankuh Mining District, 20 km South West of Esfahan city in Iran. e Irankuh Mining District (IMD) is a part of the Malayer-Esfahan Metallogenic Belt between Sanandaj and Sirjan cities1. It has been proposed that the IMD is an epigenetic Pb, Zn, and Ba Mississippi Valley-Type (MVT) according to isotopic investigations2. Later, Hoseini-Dinani and Aabi3 proposed an MVT-type genetic model based on the soil and host rock geochemical halos of Zn, Pb, Ag, Ba, Hg and Sb. Carbonate host rocks and Early Cretaceous clastic detrital form the main part of  e Gushl deposit.  e major sulphide mineralization occurs in the hanging-wall of the Gushl-Baghabrisham fault. In sulphide ore facies, there are dierent types of textures including massive, vein-veinlet, semi-massive, colloform, framboidal, and laminated4. As a processing strategy, the valued minerals are separated from the gangue minerals using the comminution process (to achieve proper liberation) and then dierential otation of galena and sphalerite. In Gushl otation plant, galena is rstly oated in the lead circuit while sphalerite and pyrite are depressed by NaCN and ZnSO4. In the zinc otation circuit, sphalerite is activated using copper sulphate and oated with specied collectors. e schematic diagram of the actual Gushl otation plant is shown in Fig. 1. In both lead and zinc circuits, pyrite is the main sulphide gangue mineral. It is critical to decrease the presence of iron (Fe) and Zn in the lead concentrate during the otation of galena. Moreover, reducing the amount of iron in the zinc concentrate is also important for making the process more economical. In addition, increasing the recovery of lead and zinc otation will decrease the adverse impact of produced tailings on the environment. In practice, this is not always easy due to the dierent behaviour of complex ores from pure single minerals. Selective otation of sulphide minerals from complex ore is dependent on the several parameters such as: type and dosage of collectors, galvanic interactions and activation by dissolved ions5–9.  erefore, depressants have been used to improve the selectivity of desired minerals by acting on a mineral surface or by reacting with other reagents such as collectors and activators10. Chitosan has been used as a selective depressant in the dierential Pb and Zn sulphide otation on synthesized sphalerite and galena mixtures11. It has been shown that, aer EDTA addition, sphalerite recovery has been decreased while galena has been oated at pH 4. It was shown that sphalerite could be activated by cuprous cyanide complexes in the lead otation circuit and it leads to the copper adsorption on the sphalerite surface. It means that higher cyanide is needed to leach out copper from the 1Department of Research and Development, Bama Mining Company, Isfahan 81747-54754, Iran. 2Institute of Research and Development, Duy Tan University, Da Nang 550000, Viet Nam. 3The Faculty of Environment and Chemical Engineering, DuyTan University, Da Nang 550000,Viet Nam. \*email: mahdighadiri@duytan.edu.vn **Scientic Reports** | (2021) 11:3103 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-82759-3 1 Vol.:( ) www.nature.com/scientificreports/ ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:2/block:2) Figure 1.  e schematic process ow diagram of actual otation plant. sphalerite surface for the ecient depression of sphalerite12. It was also indicated that sphalerite can be separated from the mixture of sphalerite—galena using dextrin as a depressant for galena at pH 1213. On the other hand, the pH of the pulp determines the surface charge of the minerals and adsorption of reagents onto the minerals that led to the selective otation of minerals from the ore14. Hence, the pH can be adjusted to act as a simple and economical depressant to achieve higher selectivity. Also, this method has less environmental problems and is regarded as the rst step in the optimization of the process5. For example, pyrite depression with lime at high pH values is one of the well-known operational conditions in the sulphide minerals otation plants15–17. In addition, to achieve better selectivity and recovery, reagent dosage plays a crucial role in the otation process.  erefore reagents specially collectors and the pH should be accurately balanced to obtain optimum grade and recovery16. Xanthate collectors are one of the most broadly used collectors for sulphide minerals otation, especially for easy- to- treat ores where selectivity against iron sulphides and penalty elements is not a critical problem5,17. Increasing the carbon chain length of xanthates increases the recovery power while lowering the selectivity18. On the other hand, the stability of these collectors at low pH decreases and hence they are not suitable for otation in acidic conditions17. Flotation behaviour of galena and mechanism of adsorption of collector on the surface of galena aer cyanide treatment has been investigated by the researchers. It was found that there is electrostatic adsorption in the interaction between butyl xanthate and the surface of galena aer cyanide treatment in the pH range 4.2–8.419.  erefore, to obtain desired metallurgical results, using other collector types or a combination of two or more dierent collectors is necessary. Phosphine-based collectors and dithiophosphates are one of the alternatives that are used in the otation of complex minerals in combination with xanthates or used individually17. Aero 3418 A and Aero 3477 are suitable options for increasing the selectivity in the lead sulphide and zinc sulphide otation circuits, respectively. Aero 3418 A has a good selectivity against iron sulphide and Aero 3477 is strong and selective for the activated zinc minerals and exhibits selectivity against the iron sulphides17.  erefore, the aim of this study is to nd the optimum pH and collector type and dosage for the galena and sphalerite otation from a complex lead–zinc ore. ## Materials and methods Materials.  e lead–zinc ore was supplied by Gushl mine, Iran. Ore samples were crushed to produce−2 mm particles using jaw and roll crushers.  en, the samples were ground in a mild steel rod mill for a certain time to achieve particle size 80% − 75 µm. All chemicals were used at industrial grade without any further purications. X-ray powder diraction (GIXRD, ASENWARE AW-XDM 300) and X-ray uorescence (XRF, Philips PW1480) were conducted on the otation feed, lead and zinc concentrates and tailing to identify the mineral content and elemental composition.  e minerals content was semi-quantitatively calculated by Rietveld-like (RIR) method. In this method, XRD and XRF analyses results were combined for determination of minerals abundance (weight percentage) in the samples20. **Scientic Reports** | (2021) 11:3103 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-82759-3 Vol:.(1234567890) 2 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:3/block:2) Figure 2.  e simple owsheet of otation tests. **The pulp pH and redox potential measurement.**  e solution pH was measured using a Metrohm 827 pH meter.  e redox potential was determined with a reference to a saturated Ag/AgCl electrode using a Pt electrode attached to a Metrohm 827 pH meter21.  e precision of the measurements was tested using a Crison standard redox solution of 250 mV at 25 °C21. ## Flotation experiment.  e otation tests were performed in self-aerated Denver otation machine with a 2.3 L cell and agitation speed was adjusted to 900 rpm.  e pH of pulp (5–11.5) and collector type in the otation cell were changed according to the experimental requirements. In the lead otation, certain amounts of depressants (zinc sulphate 400 g/ton and sodium cyanide 50 g/ton with 5 min conditioning), collector (PEX 40 g/ton or Aero3418 10 g/ton with 2 min conditioning) and frother (MIBC 20 g/ton with 1 min conditioning) were added respectively aer adjusting pH to desired values (5–11.5).  e pH of the pulp was monitored aer adding each reagent. e zinc otation tests were conducted aer determination of optimum conditions for the lead oatation. In the zinc otation experiments, aer pH adjustment, conditioning was performed by adding copper sulphate as sphalerite activator (250 g/ton for 2 min), PAX (50 g/ton) or Aero 3477 (20 g/ton) as sphalerite collector for 2 min and frother (MIBC 20 g/ton for 1 min). Aer conditioning, the otation was started with the injection of air in the otation cell, while the self-aerated regulator was kept entirely open in all the otation tests.  e otation was performed for 3 min for both lead and zinc concentrates as shown in Fig. 2, then, the otation products were weighted and analysed chemically. Using well-known equation [Eq. (1)], recoveries (or distributions) were calculated22. ![Formula block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:3/block:11) where C is the weight of lead or zinc concentrate and F is the weight of feed that here is 1 kg.  e symbols of c and f are the grades of lead, zinc or iron in the concentrates and feed, respectively. ## Kinetics study.  e kinetics experiments were conducted for both lead and zinc circuits using PEX and PAX collectors, respectively.  e experiments were carried out at pH values of 6 and 8.  e classical rst-order otation model as a standard model was used to nd kinetics parameters of lead and zinc otation circuits23,24. ![Formula block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:3/block:16) where k is the average otation rate constant, R∞ denotes the ultimate recovery, R is the recovery of desired minerals and t is the otation time. and tailing are provided in Table 1. TXRD and mineralogical studies showed that pyrite and sphalerite are the major sulphide minerals and galena is the minor sulphide mineral. Also, dolomite, barite and quartz are the major gangue minerals  e oxidation rate of lead and zinc was 11 and 5 percent respectively. Transmitted (up) and reected (down) microscopic images of the run of mine ore cross-section are shown in Fig. 3. Crystals of sphalerite, galena, and pyrite as sulphide minerals and dolomite as the main gangue mineral can be seen in Fig. 3. Some of the cracks are lled with galena and a tiny amount of bitumen minerals. ## Lead otation stage. Eect of pH on the grade and recovery of lead. PEX and Aero 3418 were used as collector.  e PEX is a common collector and is used in the Gushl plant for the galena otation.  e Aero 3418 was selected because not only it has lower anity toward depressed zinc sulphide, but also it has lower selectivity for the iron sulphide.  erefore, the eect of these collectors on the lead recovery was investigated at dierent pH values.  e results of the lead otation using PEX and Aero 3418 A at various amounts of pH was shown in Fig. 4. As can be seen, the lead grade approached the highest value at pH 8 and decreased at higher pH values for both collectors, while, the lead recovery decreased with increasing the pH. As Fig. 5 shows a substantial increase was observed in the pulp redox potential when the pH decreases from 8 to 5 which can facilitate lead recovery25. It has been reported that the otation of the pure galena takes place at pH values in the range of 2–1026.  e formation of plumbite instead of lead xanthate has been reported as a reason for the reduction of lead recovery at pH values higher than 1118 . Also, It has been shown that, Pb(OH)+ adsorbed on the galena or sphalerite surface can reduce the collector ability for the galena otation in the pH values between 7 and 9.5, but had a signicant activating eect on the sphalerite oatability in the pH range 7.5–10.527.  e lead otation in the industrial scale is usually carried out in the pH range 7 to 10.5 based on the ore mineralogy and petrogenesis16. But, as the lead grade is an important consideration, other impurities such as zinc and iron in the lead concentrate should be reduced. Zinc and iron distribution and grade in the lead concentrate.  e inuence of pH and collector type on the distribution of zinc in the lead concentrate is shown in Fig. 6. For both collectors, it was observed that the zinc distribution in the lead concentrate and its grade has a downward trend, when the pH was increased from 5 to 8. In spite of higher lead recovery at pH 5 (Fig. 4), the distribution of zinc in the lead concentrate is also higher which causes unacceptable losses of zinc in zinc concentrate.  e pH value of 8 is the optimum pH for the lead otation because the lead grade is in its maximum value and the zinc distribution in the lead concentrate is low. **Scientic Reports** | (2021) 11:3103 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-82759-3 Vol:.(1234567890) 4 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:5/block:2) Figure 3. Microscopic image of a thin section from a fragment of Gushl ore, transmitted image (up), reected image (down).  e showed minerals are sphalerite (Sp), galena (Ga), pyrite (Py), dolomite (Do), bitumen (Bit). e eect of pulp pH on the distribution and grade of iron in the lead concentrate is shown in Fig. 7. It is clearly seen that the distribution and grade of iron in the lead concentrate are lower than 10% for both collectors at pH 8. It means that the iron distribution and grade is in the acceptable range for the otation of lead. Also, Aero 3418 collector showed suitable behaviour against iron and zinc at lower pH values. As can be seen from Figs. 6 and 7, the distribution of zinc and iron in the lead concentrate increases with decreasing pH. It should be attributed to the decreasing of cyanide ion (CN−) in the pulp at lower pH value. e cyanide ion has a depressing eect on the zinc and iron sulphide15,18. In the pH range of 6 to 8.4, cyanide is volatilized and more than 90% of that occurs as hydrogen cyanide in the pulp that leads to cyanide losses from the pulp28. **Zinc otation stage.** Inuence of pH and collector type on the recovery and grade of zinc. Aer lead otation at optimum pH 8, the otation of zinc at a dierent pH (5–11.5), with two collector types, was performed to study the recovery and grade of zinc in the zinc concentrate. Figure 8 shows the grade and recovery of zinc in the zinc concentrate using PAX or Aero 3477 collectors at pH 5–11.5. It can be observed that the maximum grade and recovery for zinc were obtained at pH 6 for both collectors.  e grade and recovery of zinc were decreased from 43 to 17% and from 77 to 42% with increasing pH from 6 to 11.5 in the presence of Aero 3477 in the pulp. Hence the use of Aero 3477 at lower pH values is recommended. Fuerstenau et al.18 reported that the maximum recovery of sphalerite in the presence of PAX takes place at pH 3.5 and it decreases with increasing pH.  e increase in the zinc recovery at pH values in the range of 8–11.5 in this study can be due to the addition of copper sulphate as sphalerite activator in the pulp which has been reported by Hu et al.25.  ey reported that in absence of copper sulphate, sphalerite recovery decreases gradually from pH 3 to 8 with butyl xanthate as collector but In the presence of copper sulphate, recovery of sphalerite can be higher than 90% at pH<1225 which is in agreement with our results. Eect of pH and collector type on the iron distribution and grade in the lead concentrate. e average otation rate constant (k) and the ultimate recovery (R∞) for the lead, zinc, and iron are shown in Table 3. Changes in pH do not have a considerable eect on the average otation rate constant of lead, but, the ultimate recovery is 5% higher at pH 6. On the other hand, zinc and iron distribution are 46.28% and 16.47% at pH 6. It means, it is not logical to use this pH for the lead otation. Moreover, to increase the recovery in the lead circuit otation at pH 6, more zinc sulphate and sodium cyanide should be used to depress the zinc and iron sulphide. Figure 11 shows otation kinetic rates of zinc and iron in the zinc otation stage.  e average otation rate constant (k) and the ultimate recovery (R∞) were tabulated in Table 3. According to Table 4, the average otation rate constant of zinc at pH 6 is more than 2 times its value at pH 8.  e ultimate recovery was achieved to be 79.56% at pH 6 while it was 77.67% at pH 8.  is indicates that for cell design purposes, pH should be considered. As shown here, more recovery could be achievable with lower cell volumes due to the higher kinetics rate at pH 6. Eect of pH and collector type on the iron distribution and grade in the zinc concentrate. ## Conclusion Using optimized pH in the lead otation stage can remarkably improve the grade and recovery of lead, and prevents zinc losses in the lead concentrate and decreases iron content in it.  e distribution of zinc and iron increases at acidic pH (below 7) in the lead concentrate. A huge reduction of iron and zinc grade and distribution at pH 8 in the lead concentrate was observed. So, this pH was considered as optimum pH for the lead otation due to higher grade and proper recovery of lead. Aero 3418 A collector showed more selective behaviour for the zinc and iron in comparison with potassium ethyl xanthate in the lead otation stage. In the zinc otation stage, the grade and recovery of zinc were more acceptable at pH 6 compared with other pH values. Aero 3477 had acceptable performance at low pH values (5–7). It was shown that the pH of pulp could aect the otation kinetics of all oatable sulphides and should be considered in the designing purposes.  e results of the current study not only can improve the economical and metallurgical aspects of the process but also would solve the operational problems created in the process when working with basic pH in the zinc circuit like preparing limewater and precipitation in the tubes. **Scientic Reports** | (2021) 11:3103 | https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-021-82759-3 Vol:.(1234567890) 8 www.nature.com/scientificreports/ ![Image block](doc:9ff03d7/tier:flash/page:9/block:2)
